241.event_title: Abdul Sattar Edhi builds Pakistan's largest welfare network while living with almost nothing
241.event: In 1951 Abdul Sattar Edhi established a charitable service in Karachi, funded by private donations, to provide basic emergency care, starting with a single ambulance that he drove himself. The Edhi Foundation grew into a nationwide network of ambulances, maternity centres, orphan care and shelters, and in 1997 it entered Guinness World Records as the largest volunteer ambulance organisation. Edhi never took a salary from the foundation, owned only a couple of sets of clothes and lived in a small room beside his office.
241.explanation: Edhi became one of the most honoured people in his country through compassion alone, while deliberately possessing almost nothing.
241.tie_back: The kural calls compassion the wealth of all wealths and notes that money is found even among the base, and Edhi's life showed a person rich only in compassion yet esteemed above the wealthy.
241._accuracy_note: A strong fit for the contrast between compassion as true wealth and material wealth, though the kural's remark about wealth in base hands is not directly shown.

242.event_title: Akbar's debates in the Ibadat Khana
242.event: In 1575 the Mughal emperor Akbar began building the Ibadat Khana, a hall of worship at Fatehpur Sikri, where weekly debates were held. From 1578 he opened the discussions to Hindu pandits, Jain teachers, Zoroastrian priests and Jesuit missionaries as well as Muslim scholars. Britannica records that this comparative study convinced him that there was truth in all religions but that none possessed the whole truth, and his court developed the policy of sulh-i kul, universal peace and tolerance among creeds.
242.explanation: An emperor deliberately examined many rival doctrines side by side and arrived at a policy of tolerance and protection for all his subjects.
242.tie_back: The kural says that whatever paths one examines, compassion alone proves the true support, and Akbar's testing of many creeds led him to a policy of goodwill toward all.
242._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of Parimelazhagar's ecumenical reading (testing the doctrines of many schools), though Akbar's conclusion is framed as tolerance rather than compassion as such.

243.event_title: Corrie ten Boom survives Ravensbruck and turns to healing work
243.event: Corrie ten Boom and her family hid Jews and resistance workers in their home in Haarlem until it was raided on 28 February 1944; the six people in the hiding place were not found. Corrie was imprisoned and deported with her sister Betsie to the Ravensbruck concentration camp, where Betsie died in December 1944, and Corrie was released at the end of that month. After the war she helped run a home for camp survivors and worked at rehabilitation with former Dutch collaborators.
243.explanation: Her compassion took her into one of the darkest places of the century, yet she came out of it devoted to healing rather than to bitterness.
243.tie_back: On the modern commentators' reading of the kural, the darkness the compassionate never enter is inner misery, and ten Boom passed through a camp without being swallowed by hatred.
243._accuracy_note: Next-best only: she did literally enter a place of great suffering, so the fit depends on reading the kural's dark world as inner darkness, and her inner state is interpretation rather than documented fact.

244.event_title: The founding of the world's first animal protection society
244.event: In 1822 Parliament passed the Cruel Treatment of Cattle Act, promoted by the MP Richard Martin and often called Martin's Act, the first law protecting animals. On 16 June 1824 Martin, the Reverend Arthur Broome, William Wilberforce and others met at Old Slaughter's Coffee House in London and founded the Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals, the first national animal protection society in the world. In 1840 Queen Victoria allowed it to add Royal to its name.
244.explanation: Protection of living beings was extended beyond humans into law and organised public action for the first time.
244.tie_back: The kural praises those who protect all living beings and live by compassion, and the founders of the society made the protection of animals a public cause.
244._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: it illustrates protecting living beings, but the kural's promise that such people need not fear the consequences of their deeds is not shown.

245.event_title: The public rallies to Mary Seacole after her bankruptcy
245.event: Mary Seacole, a Jamaican-born businesswoman and healer, ran a hotel and store near the front in the Crimean War, where she fed and cared for British soldiers. At the war's end she returned to England destitute and was declared bankrupt. Military admirers raised funds for her, a benefit festival in 1857 attracted thousands of people, and her memoir Wonderful Adventures of Mrs Seacole in Many Lands, published the same year, sold well.
245.explanation: The kindness she had shown to others was publicly remembered, and the public's support lifted her out of ruin.
245.tie_back: The kural says sorrow does not stay with those who live by compassion and that the wide world stands witness, and in Seacole's case the people of the world themselves came to her aid.
245._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: her distress was real before it was relieved, so the event shows sorrow overcome with the world as witness rather than sorrow never arriving.

246.place: Massachusetts Bay Colony and Providence, New England
246.event: The Puritan colony of Massachusetts Bay, founded by people who had left England in search of freedom to worship in their own way, banished the minister Roger Williams in October 1635 for his dangerous opinions, including his view that magistrates had no right to interfere in matters of religion. Williams fled and in 1636 founded Providence on land from the Narragansett, as a refuge for people troubled in conscience. It became a haven for Baptists, Quakers, Jews and other dissenters.
246.explanation: A community shaped by the experience of religious pressure imposed the same pressure on a dissenter in its midst, while the man it expelled built a refuge for others.
246.tie_back: The kural says those who abandon compassion have forgotten what they themselves suffered, and the colony's leaders treated a dissenter as they had once complained of being treated.
246._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of moral forgetfulness of one's own past suffering, though the kural's specific reading of forgetting life's purpose is only indirectly shown.

247.event_title: Enrico Scrovegni builds the Arena Chapel painted by Giotto
247.event: Reginaldo Scrovegni of Padua was a notorious moneylender whom Dante placed among the usurers in the Inferno. His son Enrico, also a banker, founded a chapel on the site of the Roman arena in Padua around 1303, which was consecrated in 1305 and decorated by Giotto with a celebrated fresco cycle. In its Last Judgment Enrico is shown kneeling and presenting the chapel to the Virgin, while usurers appear among the damned.
247.explanation: Art historians often read the chapel as an attempt by a rich banking family to secure spiritual standing that wealth alone could not buy.
247.tie_back: The kural says wealth rules this world but compassion is the currency of the next, and the Scrovegni chapel shows a fortune made in this world being spent in hope of the other.
247._accuracy_note: Next-best: the contrast between worldly wealth and the hereafter is clear, but Enrico's motive of atonement is a scholarly interpretation, not a documented fact, and the chapel was an act of piety rather than compassion.

248.event_title: Henri Dunant, ruined and forgotten, receives the first Nobel Peace Prize
248.event: Henri Dunant, whose efforts after the Battle of Solferino led to the founding of the Red Cross, went bankrupt in 1867, left Geneva and spent years in poverty and obscurity. A journalist found him living in a hospice in the village of Heiden in 1895, and in 1901 he shared the first Nobel Peace Prize with Frederic Passy, honoured for his humanitarian efforts to help wounded soldiers. The prize money was kept from his creditors and remained untouched in a Norwegian bank when he died in 1910.
248.explanation: Dunant lost his fortune but never his compassion, and it was the compassion that the world finally honoured.
248.tie_back: The kural says those who lose wealth may flourish again, but those who lose compassion are truly destitute, and Dunant, poor but rich in compassion, flourished again in the world's esteem.
248._accuracy_note: Almost a dramatisation of the kural's first half: a man who lost his wealth blossomed again because his compassion endured.

249.event_title: The Spanish Requerimiento is read to Indigenous peoples
249.place: Spanish Americas (first read on the coast of present-day Colombia)
249.event: Around 1510-1513 the Council of Castile drew up the Requerimiento, a formal text to be read aloud to Indigenous peoples before conquest, asserting the authority of the pope and the Spanish crown and demanding their submission and acceptance of Christian preaching. It was often read only in Spanish, sometimes from a distance, so that its hearers could not understand it, and translation was merely recommended. Historians describe it as a legal formality that served chiefly to justify conquest to the Spanish themselves.
249.explanation: An outward ritual of legality and religion was performed without any real concern for the people it addressed.
249.tie_back: The kural says virtue practised without compassion is as unreal as a confused mind claiming to see the truth, and the Requerimiento was a show of righteousness emptied of any regard for its hearers.
249._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of the outward form of righteousness without inner compassion, though the act is institutional rather than one person's practice of virtue.

250.event_title: West Germany's Basic Law guarantees asylum to the politically persecuted
250.event: The Basic Law of the Federal Republic of Germany, drafted by the Parliamentary Council and proclaimed on 23 May 1949, stated in Article 16 that persons persecuted on political grounds enjoy the right of asylum. Germany's Federal Agency for Civic Education explains that the right was included because many people persecuted for racial or political reasons under the Nazi regime had survived only by finding refuge abroad, while others had been refused such protection. The provision was deliberately worded without restrictions; it was later narrowed by an amendment in 1993.
250.explanation: A new state wrote the memory of its own citizens' flight and vulnerability into a protection for the weak of other nations.
250.tie_back: The kural asks the strong to remember how they once stood helpless before the stronger, and the framers of the Basic Law turned the memory of persecution and exile into a guarantee for the persecuted.
250._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of power restrained by remembered vulnerability, though it is a collective constitutional act rather than an individual's moment of temptation.
